This post focuses on the analytic signal. The analytic-signal view is central in communications, radar, controls, and physics-based signal analysis because it separates amplitude and phase behavior in a mathematically clean way. The word “analytic” here is not a coincidence of terminology — it’s the same complex-analysis concept from a math methods course, applied on the time axis instead of the spatial or complex-variable axis it’s usually introduced with. This post builds the signal-processing machinery first, then closes the loop back to complex analysis to show why the name fits.
What “analytic” means, briefly A function $\omega(z)$ is analytic in a region if it has a derivative at every point in that region, where the derivative
$$ \frac{d\omega}{dz} = \lim_{\Delta z \to 0} \frac{\omega(z+\Delta z)-\omega(z)}{\Delta z} $$must be independent of the direction $\Delta z$ approaches zero from. Writing $\omega(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$, this path-independence is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations:
$$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} $$In other words: $u$ and $v$ aren’t independent real functions once the analytic condition is imposed — each one determines the other (up to a constant), and they’re called harmonic conjugates. Keep that pairing in mind; it’s exactly what the Hilbert transform produces below.
Real-valued signal and its analytic counterpart Let $x(t)$ be a real-valued signal. We can form the analytic signal $s(t) = x(t) + j\hat{x}(t)$, where $\hat{x}(t)$ is the Hilbert transform of $x(t)$. Its Fourier transform $S(\omega)$ is zero for $\omega < 0$ by construction.
$$ x_a(t) = x(t) + j\hat{x}(t). $$In the frequency domain,
$$ X_a(f) = \begin{cases} 2X(f), & f > 0, \\ 0, & f \le 0. \end{cases} $$So the analytic signal keeps only positive-frequency content (one-sided spectrum). This one-sidedness is often how we define an analytic signal in signal processing courses and papers.
Hilbert transform pair The Hilbert transform is
$$ \hat{x}(t) = \mathcal{H}\{x(t)\} = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x(\tau)}{t-\tau}\,d\tau. $$This integral has a problem: the denominator $t-\tau$ hits zero when $\tau = t$, so the integrand blows up right at the point we’re integrating through. To make sense of the integral, we exclude a small symmetric window of width $2\epsilon$ around $\tau = t$ and shrink it to zero after integrating:
$$ \hat{x}(t) = \frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+} \left(\int_{-\infty}^{t-\epsilon} + \int_{t+\epsilon}^{\infty}\right) \frac{x(\tau)}{t-\tau}\,d\tau. $$Because the window is symmetric, the parts of the integral that blow up on either side of $\tau=t$ cancel each other out, leaving a finite result. In practice this rarely needs to be handled explicitly — discrete implementations (FIR/IIR Hilbert filters, or the FFT-domain construction used later in this post) never evaluate the kernel exactly at $\tau=t$, so the singularity doesn’t show up numerically in practice.
The frequency-domain form follows directly, since the integral above is a convolution and convolution becomes multiplication in frequency:
$$ \hat{X}(f) = -j\,\operatorname{sgn}(f)\,X(f), $$with
$$ \operatorname{sgn}(f) = \begin{cases} 1, & f > 0, \\ 0, & f = 0, \\ -1, & f < 0. \end{cases} $$So the Hilbert transform is just a filter, $H(f) = -j,\operatorname{sgn}(f)$, that leaves magnitude alone and shifts phase by $-90°$ at positive frequencies and $+90°$ at negative frequencies — nothing more exotic than that.
$$ X_a(f) = X(f) + j\hat{X}(f) = X(f) + \operatorname{sgn}(f)X(f). $$Here’s why that combination produces a one-sided spectrum: adding $j\hat{X}(f)$ to $X(f)$ turns the $-90°$ phase shift on the positive side into constructive addition, doubling those components ($X(f)+X(f)=2X(f)$ for $f>0$), while the $+90°$ shift on the negative side produces destructive cancellation, zeroing them out entirely ($X(f)-X(f)=0$ for $f<0$). At $f=0$, $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$, so the component is left unchanged. The result is exactly the one-sided spectrum introduced earlier — the original positive-frequency content scaled by 2, and nothing at negative frequencies.
Magnitude and phase representation Let’s write the analytic signal in polar form:
$$ x_a(t) = A(t)e^{j\phi(t)}, $$where
$$ A(t) = |x_a(t)| = \sqrt{x^2(t) + \hat{x}^2(t)}, $$and
$$ \phi(t) = \arg\{x_a(t)\}. $$The original real signal is recovered by taking the real part:
$$ x(t) = \Re\{x_a(t)\} = A(t)\cos\phi(t). $$Instantaneous frequency When phase is unwrapped and differentiable, instantaneous frequency is
$$ f_i(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\phi(t)}{dt}. $$This is useful for nonstationary and narrowband signals where local frequency content evolves over time.
Connection to complex envelope For a bandpass signal centered near $f_c$, define
$$ x_a(t) = \tilde{x}(t)e^{j2\pi f_c t}, $$where $\tilde{x}(t)$ is the complex envelope (complex baseband). Therefore,
$$ \tilde{x}(t) = x_a(t)e^{-j2\pi f_c t}. $$If we write
$$ \tilde{x}(t)=x_I(t)+jx_Q(t), $$then the real passband signal can be written as
$$ x(t)=x_I(t)\cos(2\pi f_c t)-x_Q(t)\sin(2\pi f_c t). $$This decomposition is the standard I/Q representation used throughout communication and radar systems.
Short derivation for a cosine Let
$$ x(t)=\cos(2\pi f_0 t). $$Its Hilbert transform is
$$ \hat{x}(t)=\sin(2\pi f_0 t). $$Therefore,
$$ x_a(t)=\cos(2\pi f_0 t)+j\sin(2\pi f_0 t)=e^{j2\pi f_0 t}, $$which has only a positive-frequency spectral line.
This example is small enough to check the analytic condition directly. Extend $t$ to a complex variable $z = t + j\tau$ and evaluate the same formula there:
$$ x_a(z) = e^{j2\pi f_0 z} = e^{j2\pi f_0 t}\,e^{-2\pi f_0 \tau}. $$This is entire (analytic everywhere) in $z$, and for $\tau > 0$ it decays rather than blows up — well-behaved in the upper half of the complex $t$-plane. That decay for $\tau>0$ is not a coincidence of this particular example; it’s forced by $f_0 > 0$, i.e., by the one-sided spectrum. The general case below shows why.
Why the analytic signal is actually analytic Go back to the single-tone case worked out above: $x_a(t) = e^{j2\pi f_0 t}$ for a positive frequency $f_0$. Extending $t$ into the complex plane as $z = t + j\tau$ gave
$$ x_a(z) = e^{j2\pi f_0 t}\,e^{-2\pi f_0 \tau}, $$an oscillation at $f_0$ multiplied by a decaying exponential in $\tau$. That decay only happens because $f_0 > 0$. If $f_0$ were negative, the same substitution would give a term that grows without bound as $\tau$ increases.
A general analytic signal is a sum of tones like this one, weighted by $X_a(f)$, but restricted entirely to $f>0$. Tilt time into the complex plane the same way, and every one of those tones picks up a decaying factor $e^{-2\pi f\tau}$ for $\tau>0$ — none of them grow, because none of them have negative frequency. Stack up infinitely many decaying pieces and the sum stays well-behaved: it converges, and it stays smooth (differentiable) as $z$ moves around in that region. That’s the entire content of “analytic” from earlier in this post, arrived at using a physical explanation that nothing in the signal has an ingredient that blows up in that direction.
If even one negative-frequency component were present, its exponential would grow instead of decay, and the sum would diverge and the function would fail to be analytic there. So restricting to $f>0$ is precisely the condition that keeps the complex-time extension finite. $x_a(t)$ is the boundary value of that extension as $\tau \to 0^+$ — the signal you actually measure is the edge of a better-behaved function living just off the real time axis.
This should look familiar It’s the same logic as the region of convergence (ROC) for a one-sided signal’s Laplace or Z-transform: a causal signal ($x(t)=0$ for $t<0$, one-sided in time) has a transform that converges, and is therefore analytic, only in a half-plane of the complex frequency variable $s$ (or outside some radius in $z$). Here the one-sidedness is in frequency instead of time, so the roles swap: a one-sided spectrum forces the analytic condition in a half-plane of complex time. Same convergence mechanism, opposite domain.
Tying $x$ and $\hat{x}$ together On the real axis ($\tau=0$), $x_a(t) = x(t) + j\hat{x}(t)$ - the in-phase/quadrature signal. But because $x_a(z)$ is analytic, its real and imaginary parts aren’t free to be anything: the Cauchy-Riemann equations lock them into a specific pair (harmonic conjugates), and on the real axis that constraint is exactly the Hilbert transform relation between $x$ and $\hat{x}$. The Hilbert transform is the transform that falls out once you insist the spectrum is one-sided.
And the loop closes with causality Run the identical argument with time and frequency swapped: a causal impulse response $h(t)$ (zero for $t<0$) has a Fourier transform $H(\omega)$ that is analytic in the upper half of the complex $\omega$-plane, for exactly the same convergence reason. That analytic condition forces the real and imaginary parts of $H(\omega)$ into a Hilbert-transform pair of their own: the Kramers-Kronig relations. The analytic signal is the mirror image of a causal system and is one-sided in frequency instead of time, analytic in time instead of frequency.

I am developing a new Radar Signal Processing course at Utah State University (USU) for Fall 2026 semester. The course will be ECE 5930/6930 and enrollment is already fill with a mix of graduate students and senior undergraduate students.
This course is designed to develop a strong understanding of first principals and then bridge theory and practice so students can start to do real signal-processing with real noisy radar data.
Why this course? Radar sits at the intersection of electromagnetics, statistical signal processing, detection and estimation, and RF engineering. Many students encounter pieces of this puzzle in separate classes, but rarely see how the full radar processing picture fits together. The goal of this course is to connect those pieces in a way that is both rigorous and practical.
What students will learn The course will focus on core ideas and implementation-oriented skills, including:
Radar fundamentals and system-level thinking Pulse compression and matched filtering Range-Doppler processing and clutter considerations Detection concepts (CFAR and thresholding strategies) Angle estimation basics and array processing intuition Introductory tracking and state estimation concepts Imaging radar fundementals Introduction to Space-Time Adaptive Processing (STAP) We will also discuss where machine learning can help, and where classical signal processing remains the best tool.
Hands-on philosophy A key design objective is to make this a build-and-test course, not just a lecture course. Students will work through guided labs and mini-projects where they:
Simulate radar waveforms in software Implement collection and processing using hardware and software Evaluate performance with both ideal and real-world noisy radar data The intention is for students to leave with both conceptual understanding and practical confidence needed for industry or research.
Course development process Designing the course has involved balancing depth, pacing, and prerequisites. I am structuring content so that students with a course in discrete-time signals and systems can move quickly into radar-specific methods while still reinforcing signal processing first-principles.
I am also prioritizing clear visualizations and reproducible computational examples so difficult ideas become easier to internalize. Concepts will be reinforced through individual projects on labs.
Looking ahead I will share updates as the course continues to develop, including sample topics, lab ideas, and lessons learned from teaching the first offering.

In this technical post, we derive the relationship between the period of an orbit and the radius of the orbit using a simple pendulum. Then we look at how to compute azimuth and elevation angles to a satellite using orbital parameters.
Introduction It took Kepler sixteen years to derive his third law. However, given Newton’s laws, we can derive the relationship between the period of an orbit and the radius of the orbit using a simple pendulum. If we consider the period of a pendulum whose length is equal to the radius of the Earth $R_e$, we can derive a relationship between the period of an orbit and the radius of the orbit. This period has an important meaning, and we will see that it is also possible to consider other satellite orbits using the relationship derived.
The Pendulum Newton’s second law tells us that the force experienced by a body is equal to its mass times its acceleration. In the case of the pendulum in Figure 1, we can write the force component due to gravity $mg$ in the direction of acceleration as
$$ F = mg\sin\theta $$which for small angles can be approximated as
$$ F \approx mg\theta. $$The tangential acceleration of the rotating mass at the end of a massless rod is
$$ a = L\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}. $$Combining these equations gives
$$ -mg\sin\theta = mL\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} $$which can be rearranged to
$$ \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{L}\sin\theta = 0. $$ Figure 1: Simple pendulum with mass $M$ and length $L$. A solution to this differential equation is
$$ \theta(t) = \theta_0\cos(\omega t) $$where
$$ \omega = \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} $$is the angular frequency. The period of the pendulum can be computed by
$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}. $$If we assume the rod length is equal to the radius of the Earth, or $L=6358$ kilometers, and $g=9.8$ meters per second squared, the period is approximately $5,061$ seconds, or about $84.4$ minutes. This is known as the Schuler period, and is also the orbital period of a satellite orbiting a spherical Earth of radius $L=6358$ kilometers at sea level. If we increase $L$, the orbital period gets longer.
Satellites Up to this point, we used $g=9.8\ \frac{m}{s^2}$ for acceleration due to gravity. However, this is only true at Earth’s surface and changes for larger orbit distances. Using Newton’s full expression for gravitational force between two objects:
$$ F = \frac{GM_sM_e}{R_e^2} $$where $G$ is the gravitational constant and $M_e$ and $M_s$ are the masses of the Earth and satellite. Notice that $g$ is shorthand for $\frac{GM_e}{R_e^2}$.
We can now write the period of an orbit at radius $L$ from the center of a spherical Earth as
$$ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R_e}{\frac{GM_e}{R_e^2}}}. $$This shows the relationship between period and radius:
$$ T \propto R_e^3 $$which is Kepler’s third law.
As an additional example, if we want a period of $24$ hours ($86,400$ seconds), we can solve for the pendulum length. The result is approximately $42,250$ kilometers, which is near the radius of a geostationary orbit (GEO) in the equatorial plane.
Orbital Parameters Elliptical orbits are typically defined using six Keplerian parameters. The first three are:
Semi-major axis $a$ Eccentricity $e$ (with $e=0$ for a circular orbit) Time $t_0$ at which the object is at a defined orbital position (for example, time of perigee) These three define the orbit in the two-dimensional orbital plane.
Figure 2: The elliptical orbit. The remaining parameters place that orbit in three-dimensional space:
Inclination $i$ Argument of perigee $\omega$ Right ascension $\Omega$ Figure 3: The orbit plane. Satellite Relative Position Given an Earth-station geodetic position (latitude/longitude), it is useful to compute the relative position of a satellite, star, or other object in terms of angles and distance. For example, the following two-step process can be used for a GPS satellite.
Step 1: compute the mean anomaly $M$ as
$$ M = M_0 + \frac{d\omega}{dt}(t-t_0) $$where $M_0$ is the mean anomaly at a reference time $t_0$ (epoch), and $\frac{d\omega}{dt}$ is the angular velocity.
Then solve Kepler’s equation for eccentric anomaly $E$:
$$ M = E - e\sin E $$This equation is nonlinear in $E$, so it is solved iteratively (for example with Newton’s method).
The position of the satellite in the orbital plane is
$$ x_0 = a(\cos E - e) $$$$ y_0 = a(1-e^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sin E $$$$ r = (x_0^2 + y_0^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} $$where $a$ is the semi-major axis length.
Step 2: use inclination $i$, right ascension $\Omega$, and argument of perigee $\omega$ to transform from the perifocal coordinate system to the geocentric coordinate system:
$$ P_x = \cos\omega\cos\Omega - \sin\omega\sin\Omega\cos i $$$$ P_y = \cos\omega\sin\Omega + \sin\omega\cos\Omega\cos i $$$$ P_z = \sin\omega\sin i $$$$ Q_x = -\sin\omega\cos\Omega - \cos\omega\sin\Omega\cos i $$$$ Q_y = -\sin\omega\sin\Omega + \cos\omega\cos\Omega\cos i $$$$ Q_z = \cos\omega\sin i $$The satellite position in geocentric coordinates is then
$$ x = P_xx_0 + Q_xy_0 $$$$ y = P_yx_0 + Q_yy_0 $$$$ z = P_zx_0 + Q_zy_0 $$Finally, the following equations can be used to compute satellite azimuth and elevation from a specified Earth station:
$$ \text{Right Ascension},\ \alpha = \arctan(y/x) $$$$ \text{Declination},\ \delta = \arctan\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right) $$$$ \text{Elevation},\ \eta = \arctan\left(\frac{\sin\eta_s - \frac{R}{r}}{\cos\eta_s}\right) $$with
$$ \eta_s = \arcsin\left[\sin\delta\sin\theta_e + \cos\delta\cos\theta_e\cos\phi_{se}\right]. $$where:
$R$: Earth radius $r$: satellite distance from Earth center $\theta_e$: earth station latitude $\phi_{se} = \phi_s - \phi_e$ $\phi_s$: satellite longitude $\phi_e$: earth station longitude Azimuth can be computed by
$$ A = \arctan\left[\frac{\sin\phi_{se}}{\cos\theta_e\tan\delta - \sin\theta_e\cos\phi_{se}}\right] $$and the slant range from Earth station to satellite is
$$ \rho = \sqrt{r^2 - R^2\cos^2\eta} - R\sin\eta. $$There are important correction rules for northern and southern hemispheres, and for whether the satellite lies east or west of the Earth station. In practice, these are quadrant corrections for azimuth. Those corrections are implemented in the MATLAB code included in the appendix.
Conclusion We related the period of a pendulum with a very long rod length $L$ to the period of a satellite orbit with radius $L$. Then we outlined how to compute satellite azimuth and elevation from a known earth station location.
References https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pendulum https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_period Kayton and Fried, Avionics Navigation Systems David Ohm, Modern Navigation Notes Appendix MATLAB source file used in this report: gps_azel.m
description: A technical note deriving orbit-period relationships from pendulum dynamics and outlining satellite azimuth and elevation calculations.
title: Pendulums and Orbits

One of my new hobbies is what I call antenna spotting: walking around and identifying real communications antennas in the wild.
This semester, I took students from my ECE5660 class (Communications Theory I) outside to walk around the campus area and spot, classify, and discuss antennas in real deployment settings. I also assigned a project for students to do the same thing around town.
The response was excellent. Students found the activity practical, memorable, and much more informative than seeing antennas only in slides.
Why this has been so useful Antenna theory can feel abstract until you see hardware mounted on real buildings, poles, towers, and infrastructure. Once students start connecting radiation concepts, polarization, frequency bands, and deployment constraints to physical systems, the course material becomes much more intuitive.
In these walks and projects, students practiced asking questions like:
What service might this antenna support? What frequency range is likely being used? What clues suggest omnidirectional versus directional behavior? What tradeoffs were likely made in placement and mounting? Class activity and project approach The campus walk gave students a guided starting point with immediate discussion. The follow-on project, where I asked them to go find at least seven antennas in the wild around town, pushed them to observe independently and reason from real evidence.
Typical outcomes included:
Better recognition of common antenna form factors Stronger system-level thinking about technologies and coverage More confidence connecting theory to engineering practice My new field journal Below are some of the antennas I spotted in the area. Can you guess the function, operating frequency range, and type of antenna?
Examples spotted around campus and home These are examples of antennas spotted around the university campus and my home area.

A few antennas on the college of business building. If you do this kind of antenna spotting too, I highly recommend it. It is like bird watching for communications engineers.

In this post I work through the question: can a quantum RF receiver replace my traditional receiver? I had a perfect excuse to answer it. I was building a downlink for the GOES-R geosynchronous weather satellite, and the link budget was tight enough to make any noise-floor improvement worth chasing. So I looked hard at Rydberg-atom receivers, did the math, and came away with a nuanced answer. This post walks you through what I found, with equations, scaling laws, and a couple of scripts you can run yourself.
The Motivating Problem The GOES-R broadcast is BPSK at a carrier of 1694.1 MHz with a symbol rate of 927 ksps, transmit EIRP around 78 dBm, and a path loss at 36,000 km of 188.2 dB. With a 20 dBi antenna, 8 dB noise figure, and ~5 dB of miscellaneous losses, the receiver SNR works out to roughly 6.8 dB in the signal bandwidth. That’s workable with Reed-Solomon plus rate-1/2 convolutional coding, but it is not excessive. If a quantum receiver could shave even a few dB off the noise floor for this application, it would be interesting to know. What Is a Rydberg Atom, and Why Would I Use One as a Receiver?
A Rydberg atom is an alkali atom (rubidium and cesium are the popular choices) that has been laser-excited into a state with a very high principal quantum number, typically $n > 30$. The valence electron ends up far from the ionic core, which makes the atom huge (the atomic radius scales as $r_n \propto n^2 a_0$) and gives it an enormous electric dipole moment. That, in turn, makes the atom sensitive to RF electric fields. The scaling laws matter here, because they tell you what a receiver built on these atoms can and cannot do:
$$ \mu \propto n^{2}, \quad \alpha \propto n^{7}, \quad \tau \propto n^{3} $$The dipole moment $\mu$ grows as $n^2$, the polarizability $\alpha$ as $n^7$, and the atomic lifetime $\tau$ as $n^3$. Big dipoles are what give you field sensitivity, but the long lifetimes also set a speed limit that will come back to bite us later. Figure 1. Natural Rydberg transition frequencies for Cs and Rb as a function of principal quantum number n. The red band marks the GOES-R downlink at 1.694 GHz. How the Receiver Actually Works
The typical setup is a four-level atomic system driven by two optical fields. For rubidium, a probe laser at $\lambda_p \approx 780$ nm excites atoms out of the ground state, and a counter-propagating coupling laser at $\lambda_c \approx 480$ nm pumps them into the Rydberg state. Two quantum-optical effects let you read out an RF field applied to the vapor cell: Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT), which creates a narrow transmission window in the probe, and, when the RF is on resonance with a Rydberg transition, AC-Stark-induced Autler-Townes splitting of that window. The frequency separation of the split peaks is linear in the applied field:
$$ |E| = \frac{2\pi \hbar}{\mu}\,\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_c}\,\Delta f_m $$ Figure 2. RF Quantum sensing setup showing pump (red) and coupling (blue) lasers propagating through a vapor cell. Because $\mu$ can be computed from first principles to better than 0.1% using a tool like the open-source ARC Alkali Rydberg Calculator, the measurement is self-calibrating in a way that no thermal-noise receiver is. The atoms transduce AM directly onto the probe absorption, FM becomes a linear intensity change when you park the coupling laser on the slope of the EIT peak, and phase can be recovered by running the vapor cell as a Rydberg atom mixer. In that last configuration, an RF local oscillator and the signal beat inside the atoms to produce an intermediate-frequency photocurrent:
$$ I_p \propto \left|E_{LO} + E_{SIG}\right|^2 = E_{LO}^2 + E_{SIG}^2 + 2E_{LO}E_{SIG}\cos(\Delta\omega t + \phi_{sig}) $$That is an honest-to-goodness atomic heterodyne detector, with all the usual sensitivity benefits, but the “sluggishness” of the atoms sets the maximum BPSK symbol rate you can still resolve. Figure 3. AM and FM detection schemes. Thermal Noise vs. Quantum Shot Noise
A traditional receiver is thermal-noise limited: $N_T = k_B T \Delta f$, which for a BPSK signal filtered to its symbol rate $R_s$ becomes $N_T = k_B T R_s$. A Rydberg receiver is not thermal-noise limited at all — its floor is set by quantum shot noise in the photodiode reading out the probe laser. Written in terms of the same symbol rate, the minimum detectable signal power is approximately
$$ P_{min}^{\text{Rydberg}} \approx \frac{3 h c^2 R_s^{\,2}}{8\pi Z_0 f^{\,2} N_a \wp_{34}^{\,2}} $$and the corresponding minimum detectable field, when the measurement time is shorter than the atomic relaxation time, is
$$ E_{min} = \frac{h R_s}{\wp_{34}\, N_a^{1/2}} $$where $N_a \sim 5\times10^{5}$ is the number of atoms participating. Plot these two noise floors against each other and you find a crossover in the neighborhood of $R_s \approx 1$ Msps. Below that, the atoms win; above it, thermal beats quantum. For the GOES-R case at 927 ksps, the arithmetic says there is something like a 3 dB advantage for the Rydberg receiver. That is real, but it is not free. Figure 4. Comparison of thermal noise vs quantum shot noise over a range of BPSK symbol rates. Code on associated github repository. The Frequency Coverage Catch
A two-photon EIT ladder in rubidium or cesium naturally gets you to D states ($L=2$). The transitions into and out of those states give you excellent coverage in the tens of GHz, but they do not put a natural resonance anywhere near 1.694 GHz. To land on that frequency you have to climb one rung higher, into F and G states ($L=3,4$). Quantum-mechanical selection rules ($\Delta L = \pm 1$) only let you reach them from D via another photon, which means adding an RF “dressing” field, and for this target the dressing field lives around 100 GHz. That is not a casual addition to the benchtop. It is an expensive, phase-stable, millimeter-wave source that drags the whole system into a different cost and complexity regime. Figure 5. Dressing and signal frequencies required to reach F-G transitions across n. Getting to 1.694 GHz as a signal frequency forces the dressing field up near 100 GHz. Limitations and Conclusion
Even with dressing, a single Rydberg receiver is limited to under about 10 MHz of instantaneous bandwidth because the signal has to sit inside the EIT linewidth. Above ~1 Msps the thermal-noise floor of a well-designed conventional receiver is lower. The system is not continuously tunable the way a superheterodyne front-end is; every band of interest wants its own choice of $n$, and sometimes its own dressing source. There is no simple analog AGC, because too much RF power drives EIT into a non-linear splitting regime. Conventional receivers depend on stable clocks; Rydberg receivers depend on stable lasers, and swapping one expensive dependency for another is not automatic progress.
So, do I still need my traditional receiver? For GOES-R, yes. The ~3 dB advantage does not survive contact with the 100 GHz dressing requirement and the 10 MHz bandwidth limit. But the quantum receiver has a real place in the toolbox. Space communications, small-aperture regimes where thermal noise floors and antenna losses dominate, and low-frequency applications where a long atomic integration time is fine — those are exactly the niches where a self-calibrating, SI-traceable, antenna-less E-field sensor starts to look attractive. Try It Yourself
The physics in this post is easy to play with. All Python scripts are available in the project repository on GitHub. The physics in this post is easy to play with. The Python scripts in the project directory use the ARC Alkali Rydberg Calculator to plot Rydberg energy levels, compute dipole moments for a chosen transition, search for natural transitions near a target frequency, and reproduce the Figures. Run plot_rydberg_levels.py to see the density of states grow with $n$, run rb_dipoles.py to get the dipole moments for the transitions in the paper this post is based on, and run freq_search.py with your own target frequency to find candidate transitions in cesium. Have fun!
description: A practical look at whether a Rydberg-atom quantum receiver can outperform a conventional RF front-end on a real satellite link.

In the past, I have captured signals at 137.1 MHz from the NOAA 19 weather satellite using a discone antenna without any pointing. It was exciting to see weather images appear on the computer monitor after processing the signals. At the time, I planned to find a way to set up a tracking capability so I could track the satellites while pointing a higher gain antenna at them to get better signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and longer collection time. Well, I have finally put together a system that can do this for L-band and UHF frequencies. A system adequate for x-band is in the works.
First Collect of GOES-18 For my first test using the Discovery Dish with the Az/El positioner, I decided to point at a relatively fixed satellite: GOES-18.
GOES-18 is a geostationary weather satellite, so from my location it appears at a nearly fixed azimuth and elevation. That makes it a good first target when validating the full receive chain.
For this setup, I am focused on L-band downlink collection (roughly the 1.69 GHz weather downlink region used by GOES products in many hobby workflows), then decoding and post-processing into viewable images.
Collection Setup The first step was getting the hardware chain stable: dish, feed, low-noise receive path, SDR, and computer pipeline. I also wanted a deck-level view but this turned out to be less than ideal due to added thermal noise from the house.
Fig 1. Deck-level installation view of the receive system. Fig 2. GOES-18 receive setup moved to backyard away from the house. Signal collection After pointing and calibration, the next check is signal presence and quality at the SDR. At this stage I am looking for enough SNR margin for synchronization and decode. I used the open-source SatDump application for collection and processing.
Fig 3. The SatGazer application (Mac) was used to predict satellite position and antenna pointing. Fig 4. View of SatDump screen while capturing downlink. Processed world views Once signal was captured, various weather imagery products could be processed from the data and output for viewing. These include full-world style views and enhanced products useful for weather context.
Fig 5. ABI false-color processed view. Fig 6. Clean longwave IR window product. Fig 7. Mid-level tropospheric water vapor product. There are more products and examples to show, but I will stop here. I started working on my own GOES-18 signal processing and decoding software, so I will add details about that to the post later. In addition, I plan to share more information about the antenna and positioner setup.

If you plan to dive into a Radio Frequency (RF) project, getting familiar with a few core antenna types is essential. Choosing or designing the right antenna is one of the most fundamental skills in electrical engineering, and understanding the first principles behind them will help you move quickly from concept to a working system that transmits and receives reliably.
Parabolic Dish: The dish diameter $D$ determines the gain.
$$ G = \eta (\pi D / \lambda)^2 ,$$where $\eta$ is the antenna efficiency (typically 0.45 - .70). Each doubling of the dish diameter increases the gain by $6dB$.
The beamwidth for a given frequency (or wavelength) is also determined by the diameter.
$$ \text{Beamwidth} \approx \frac{70\lambda}{D}$$The dish will work effectively for any frequency where $D \gg \lambda$. The surface accuracy also matters, especially above 10 GHz:
$$ \text{RMS surface error} \le \lambda/16$$The required $G/T$ (from your link budget) determines the gain needed. For example, if you want to receive an L-band signal at 1680 MHz from the GOES-18 weather satellite in geostationary orbit, you might want around 24 dBi of antenna gain.
$$ D = \frac{\lambda}{\pi} 10^\frac{24 - 10\log_{10}(\eta)}{20}$$Using $\lambda = 0.178$ m, $\eta = 0.6$.
$$ D \approx 0.68 \text{m} .$$It is also important to know where to place the feed. For a direct focus configuration, the focal length is
$$ F = \frac{D^2}{16c} ,$$where $F$ is the focal length and $c$ is the dish depth (measured from the center to the plane of the rim).
Perhaps the single most important geometric parameter of a dish antenna is the F/D ratio (focal length divided by diameter). This parameter determines the required feed pattern.
To understand this, imagine the feed transmitting a beam toward the dish. The feed’s illumination pattern must match the dish geometry:
If the beam is too wide → spillover occurs, and the feed sees warm ground noise, raising the system temperature. If the beam is too narrow → under-illumination reduces gain. Thus, the feed type is directly tied to the F/D ratio. More details are available in antenna-design references, but they are not covered here.
Example: Discovery Dish (L-band) Let’s look at an example like the Discovery Dish used for ameature L-band weather satellite reception. The dish diameter is 70 cm and the depth is 12 cm, giving
$$F/D = 0.36 .$$The half illumination angle is
$$ \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{D/2}{F}\right) = 53.6^\circ ,$$so the full illumination is
$$ 2\theta \approx 107^\circ .$$Typically, we want the spillover to be less than 5%, so a feed with a beamwidth of approximately 105 degrees at 1680 MHz is appropriate. This is very wide, so a patch antenna, helical feed or simple PCB feed works well.
However, remember that spillover is often the dominant noise source after LNA noise figure. The sky temperature is roughly 3 K, while the ground is around 280 K, so even modest spillover can add more noise than the LNA itself at L-band.
Here is a picture of my Discovery Dish setup during initial testing of a rotator controller.
Fig 1. My Discovery Dish setup. Sensitivity and System Temperature For receiveing weak signals, everything comes down to sensitivity:
$$ \text{Sensitivity} = \frac{G}{T_{system}} .$$$G$ depends on the effective aperture controlled illumination, while $T_{system}$ depends heavily on the spilloever noise and LNA noise figure. Good feed matching, proper illumination, and low spilloever are key to maximizing performance.

content:
This post describes my teaching and mentoring approach that has evolved over the past decade through mentoring new engineering hires and summer interns. The approach emphasizes system-level thinking, project-driven learning, and just-in-time introduction of theoretical principles, with the aim of bridging the gap between classroom instruction and the realities of engineering practice.
The method unfolds in four stages: establishing a vision, decomposing into subsystems, cycling between systems and principles, and validating through demonstration. Start with a Vision Learning begins with an ambitious project vision that establishes motivation and orients students/interns toward a “system-first” perspective. A compelling vision provides a unifying anchor that makes learning more meaningful.
For example, a motivating vision might be: “Let’s build a radar payload for a drone and use it to detect moving vehicles, drones, and people.” This type of challenge immediately connects to real-world systems and sparks curiosity.
By contrast, a limited goal such as “Let’s simulate a radar signal and then write a program to compute and plot a spectrogram” may build technical skill but risks feeling abstract and disconnected. Smaller exercises have value, but their meaning is magnified when embedded within a larger challenge.
Decompose into Subsystems Large projects naturally break into subsystems, each of which serves as an entry point for targeted instruction. When students encounter barriers, mentors can introduce the relevant first principles, ensuring that theory is tied to larger challenges.
For instance, a radar payload for a drone can be divided into:
RF front-end design and antennas Waveform design and selection Digital signal processing for detection and tracking Embedded computing and control Power management and integration with the airframe Data links and communications Test, calibration, and validation procedures Each subsystem provides opportunities to zoom in on fundamentals while maintaining momentum toward the overall system vision.
Iterative Cycle of Action The approach follows a cycle that alternates between system-level challenges and principle-level instruction. Students first encounter a system obstacle, then learn the underlying principles needed to address it, integrate the solution, and return to the system view where new challenges emerge.
In this way, principles appear as direct answers to student-driven questions, making them more relevant and memorable.
Demonstration and Validation Regular integration, testing, and demonstration are essential. Demonstrations expose weaknesses, foster resilience, and reinforce collaboration. They also provide milestones that build confidence and accountability, showing students that their work has tangible impact.
Learning Stages and Benefits The method cultivates growth across several dimensions:
Immersion — Engagement comes from pursuing a coherent project vision rather than isolated tasks. Integration — Students acquire practical skills aligned with professional expectations. Authenticity — Projects mirror the realities of engineering practice. Resilience — Students learn to face ambiguity and resolve challenges through iteration. Confidence — Students develop the ability to confront and solve complex, open-ended problems. Conclusion Not every course or program is suited to this model. Foundational instruction in mathematics, physics, and core engineering theory remains indispensable and is often best delivered through traditional approaches. However, when students have opportunities to engage in courses centered on ambitious, system-level projects—ideally not only in a senior capstone but earlier in their studies — they experience a context that more closely resembles professional engineering practice.
Such experiences can help students and interns develop confidence in applying theory to open-ended problems and strengthen their motivation to learn. They also create natural bridges between academic learning and real-world engineering challenges. For departments, this approach may encourage greater student engagement, contributing over time to a richer leerning environment.

Observing satellites in the night sky can be a fun way to learn about orbital dynamics and learn your way around the earth and sky. This discussion is specific to observers in the northern hemisphere since I am currently living in the Rocky Mountain West area.
First, let’s review some important terminology:
Azimuth is the horizontal angle, measured in degrees, from true north in a clockwise direction. The star Polaris lies within one degree of true north and is therefore a useful reference point for determining azimuth in the night sky. To locate Polaris, first find the Big Dipper (Ursa Major) and identify the two stars that form the far edge of the dipper’s cup. Extending an imaginary line through these stars about five times their spacing will point to Polaris, a magnitude~+2 star. Because of the geometry of Earth’s rotation, Polaris appears at an altitude approximately equal to the observer’s latitude.
Altitude is the angular distance measured in degrees above the local horizon. Generally, altitude can be a little tricky to estimate by eye due to terrain and the fact that people often underestimate altitude the higher the the object is in the sky.
Coordinates are the latitude and longitude of your observing location on earth. You can look these up online, or use a GPS receiver to estimate them.
Time the local time of your observation window in a standard time format (e.g., UTC)
One of the best websites for predicting when you can observe satellites is https://heavens-above.com. After entering your location, you can browse upcoming passes filtered by brightness (magnitude), azimuth, and elevation. The site also provides detailed pass information for each satellite, including when and where it will appear in the sky, its maximum altitude, and the path it will follow overhead. Figure 1 shows the list of satellites visible from my location this evening (filtered for magnitude +3 or brighter). Figure 2 illustrates the detailed viewing geometry for one of these passes, which appears in the northwestern portion of the sky.
Fig 1. Results from a query on satellites viewable at my location. Fig 2. Satellite path prediction for a satellite predicted to be viewable from my location. Viewability - Brightness using Magnitude System Astronomers measure the brightness of stars using the magnitude scale. Lower or negative numbers mean brighter objects.
For reference:
The Sun is about –27 mag, The full Moon about –12.5 mag, Sirius (the brightest nighttime star) about –1.5 mag, And the faintest stars visible to the unaided eye under dark skies are around +6 mag. Knowing a few benchmark magnitudes is helpful when estimating how bright a satellite will appear, and for judging how good your viewing conditions are. In the Northern Hemisphere, Ursa Minor is a convenient guide because it is circumpolar and contains stars ranging from about +2 to +6 mag. Optical equipment lets you see much fainter objects. A good 50 mm binocular can extend visibility from about +6 mag to around +10 mag. A 6–8 inch reflector telescope can reach roughly +14 mag, although its smaller field of view makes tracking more challenging. Following a satellite through a telescope typically requires a motorized mount and accurate orbital data. Even with current USSPACECOM tracking elements, pointing errors of up to one degree are common.

In this post, I provide short notes on how an LTI system changes the magnitude and phase of a signal.
Response of an LTI system to a complex sinusoid Start with a complex sinusoidal input:
$$ x(n) = e^{j\omega_0 n}. $$For an LTI system with impulse response $h(k)$, the output is
$$ y(n) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h(k)x(n-k) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h(k)e^{j\omega_0(n-k)}. $$Factor out the term that does not depend on $k$:
$$ y(n) = e^{j\omega_0 n}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h(k)e^{-j\omega_0 k} = e^{j\omega_0 n}H(\omega_0). $$So the output is a complex sinusoid at the same frequency as the input, multiplied by the complex value $H(\omega_0)$.
Interpretation:
$$ x(n) \rightarrow \boxed{LTI} \rightarrow y(n) = H(\omega_0)x(n) $$where $H(\omega)$ is the frequency response of the LTI system evaluated here at $\omega = \omega_0$.
Magnitude and phase form Write the frequency response in polar form:
$$ H(\omega_0) = |H(\omega_0)|e^{j\arg \left[ H(\omega_0) \right] } . $$Then
$$ y(n) = |H(\omega_0)|e^{j\left(\omega_0 n + \arg \left[ H(\omega_0) \right] \right)} . $$This shows the key result:
The amplitude is scaled by $|H(\omega_0)|$. The phase is shifted by $\arg \left[ H(\omega_0)\right]$. Eigenfunction viewpoint The complex sinusoid
$$ \psi(n) = e^{j\omega n} $$is an eigenfunction of an LTI system $\mathcal{H}$, with eigenvalue
$$ \lambda = H(\omega), $$because it satisfies
$$ \mathcal{H}\{\psi(n)\} = \lambda\psi(n). $$Equivalently,
$$ e^{j\omega n} \rightarrow \boxed{H} \rightarrow H(\omega)e^{j\omega n}. $$Why this matters for signal decomposition If we represent an arbitrary input as a weighted sum of complex sinusoids,
$$ x(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{M} a_k e^{j\omega_k n}, $$then each sinusoidal component is scaled by its corresponding frequency response value. The output of the LTI system is then
$$ y(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{M} a_k H(\omega_k)e^{j\omega_k n}. $$So the output is still a weighted sum of complex sinusoids, but the weights are modified by the system response at each frequency.
That is the core reason frequency-domain analysis is so useful: convolution in time corresponds to multiplication of spectral components by $H(\omega)$.
description: Notes on how LTI systems scale magnitude and shift phase of complex sinusoids, and why eigenfunction expansions turn convolution into multiplication.
title: LTI System Magnitude and Phase

This is a short note on how to set the noise level in a simulation to hit a desired SNR.
Let
$$ \sigma_s^2 = \text{var(signal)}, \quad \sigma_w^2 = \text{var(noise)}. $$Then SNR in dB is
$$ SNR_{dB} = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{\sigma_s^2}{\sigma_w^2}\right). $$If you generate unit-variance noise $w[n]$ and scale it by a constant $p$ (so noise is $pw[n]$), then
$$ SNR_{dB} = 20\log_{10}\left(\frac{\sigma_s}{p\sigma_{w}}\right) $$which gives
$$ p = \frac{\sigma_s}{10^{SNR_{dB}/20} \cdot \sigma_{w}}. $$For unit-variance noise, $\sigma_{w} \approx 1$, so this reduces to a very simple scaling rule.
MATLAB snippet (random BPSK) rng(1); % Parameters N = 1e5; % number of symbols snrDbTarget = 8; % desired SNR in dB % Random BPSK: bits -> symbols in {-1, +1} bits = randi([0 1], N, 1); s = 2*bits - 1; % Signal standard deviation sigmaS = std(s); % Unit-variance white Gaussian noise w = randn(N,1); sigmaW = std(w); % Scale factor to achieve target SNR p = sigmaS / (10^(snrDbTarget/20) * sigmaW); % Noisy received signal r = s + p*w; % Measured SNR noiseActual = r - s; snrDbMeasured = 10*log10(var(s) / var(noiseActual)); fprintf('Target SNR: %.2f dB\n', snrDbTarget); fprintf('Measured SNR: %.2f dB\n', snrDbMeasured); The measured SNR should be close to the target SNR, with small variation due to finite sample size.
description: A short note on converting SNR targets into noise scaling for simulated signals, with a MATLAB BPSK example.
title: SNR for Simulated Signals

This post curates my lessons learned while building and running a small tech startup from 2014 to 2022. During that time, I kept a journal of the most important lessons I learned from starting and serving as CEO of KickView Corporation for 8 years. It was, without question, a challenging and rewarding period of my career. Hopefully, others can benefit from the lessons I learned along the way.
The most important lesson One of the best things about doing a startup is the people - the ones you work with and the ones you meet along the way. I would say the experience helped me connect with people in ways that were not possible while I was an engineer at an established company. When you are the founder of a startup, you quickly learn the value of a wide variety of skills needed for running a business - accounting, legal services, commercial real estate, janitorial services, construction and building maintenance, administration, marketing, business development, etc. There are so many talents and skills needed to make the business world function, and engineering is only one small piece of that apparatus. It was humbling (in a good way) to meet so many talented and hard-working people adding value through their various skills and domain expertise. So, my first lesson learned (and most important) is to stay humble, appreciate and respect other people, and embrace the opportunity to interact with and learn from others.
Business for engineering dummies The next most important lesson is learn about basic business finance and accounting! Ideally, you want to do some of that work prior to starting a business, but it is also a fact that you can only learn some things by actually doing them. Similar to learning how to parent, your startup will be unique enough from other businesses that you will need to do some “learning on the job” in order to master it. However, that does not mean ignoring the basics. So, you will need to understand how to do some basic accounting, forecasting, and how to create and understand a balance sheet, profit-and-loss statement, and cap table (if you are raising money). I was surprised by how creative the financial aspects of the job turned out to be. It was actually more like engineering than I expected. You get to create processes and data analysis methods that work best for your business. Embrace it!
Lessons of credibility I am proud of the fact that KickView started from scratch and was profitable every year after the first year, with revenue increasing each year. After the second year, it became a multi-million dollar per year business, and we never experienced a year without significant revenue increase. The reason I mention this is that revenue is something that can be measured and correlated with business progress. It is by no means the only metric that can be measured, and I would also say it is short-sighted to say it defines success. I use it here only to provide some credibility to the lessons I want to tell you about next.
Who is who in the zoo? I am sure this phrase “who is who in the zoo” can be attributed to someone else, but I first heard it from a mentor. When I started KickView, I engaged with an attorney at a large firm in Boulder, Colorado to help with setting up the corporate documents. After the documents were in place, I asked my corporate attorney if she would introduce me to a handful of entrepreneurs in the area that had started tech companies. My goal was twofold: find a mentor, and find some potential investors.
I was introduced to several people by my attorney, and one person became both a mentor and angel investor. This relationship also turned into a friendship that lasts to this day. That mentor told me that there are four buyers in any transaction: the mentor, the financial buyer, the technical buyer, and the user buyer. He told me that it was very important to identify these buyers as soon as possible when initiating a relationship with other customers or organizations. I won’t go into details about this here, but I found through experience that this is actually true. When I could identify these buyers (actual individuals), business interactions and deals went more smoothly. My next lesson learned builds on this concept: the financial buyer and the user buyer are the most important. Do not waste all your time talking to the engineering buyer - he/she most likely wants to build or offer what you are trying to sell.
What is cultural fit? You will hear the term cultural fit mentioned a lot when talking about hiring for a startup. What does it actually mean? I will tell you that it does not mean that a hire should be interested in the same things, have similar skills, or be someone you want to be friends with. In fact, you should try to hire people that challenge your ideas and skill level regardless of how fun they are to hang out with. What you do not want is someone that has a huge ego, no humility and cannot suffer being challenged themselves. Don’t hire someone that is toxic to others just because they are brilliant. It will not be worth it.
The journey is the destination It can be easy to spend all your time thinking about where you want to be in 6 months, a year, 2 years, etc., and forget to focus on the now. When it comes to building a company, a team, and a technology, the journey can be very rewarding and often a lot of fun. Although headlines like to talk about the VC raise, the acquisition, the IPO, and revenue projections, when you talk to founders in person they love to talk about the experiences, the struggles, and the hard work along the way. Life is most enjoyable when we have unique experiences with interesting people. That can be accomplished on journeys that end with a wide range of outcomes.
description: A running journal of the most important lessons learned while starting and leading KickView Corporation for eight years.
title: Startup Lessons Learned
